sources: Australian Museum, Red Kangaroo: males up to 92 kg; males usually orange-red, females often blue-grey; one baby at a time, the size of a jellybean at birth, which climbs straight into the pouch; joeys permanently leave the pouch at about 235 days; females can delay the birth of their next baby until the previous joey has left the pouch (embryonic diapause); https://australian.museum/learn/animals/mammals/red-kangaroo/

National Geographic, Red Kangaroo: world's largest marsupial, about 200 pounds; over 35 miles an hour; can cover 25 feet in a single leap and jump 6 feet high; males box rivals, leaning back on their tails and striking with their strong hind legs; https://www.nationalgeographic.com/animals/mammals/facts/red-kangaroo

UNSW Sydney news (2014), Kangaroos use tail as fifth leg (Dawson et al., Biology Letters): when grazing on all fours, red kangaroo tails provide about as much propulsive force as the front and hind legs combined; https://www.unsw.edu.au/newsroom/news/2014/07/kangaroos-use-tail-as-fifth-leg

Taronga Conservation Society Australia, What Personal Space?: red kangaroos can produce two different types of milk at once for a joey in the pouch and another on the ground; a female can become pregnant again while a joey is still in the pouch; https://taronga.org.au/news/2018-07-11/what-personal-space

Frontiers for Young Minds (2024), co-authored at the University of Queensland, on kangaroo cooling: kangaroos spread saliva on their forearms, where a large network of blood vessels lies under thin skin, and the evaporating saliva cools them like sweat; https://kids.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/frym.2024.1333636
